items.title: Achilles can never catch the tortoise
items.claim: Zeno's paradox: Achilles gives the tortoise a head start. To catch it, he must reach where the tortoise was — by then the tortoise has moved a bit. Repeat infinitely. He performs infinitely many tasks and can never reach the tortoise.

options.text: Achilles is actually slower than the tortoise
Infinitely many finite tasks can take finite total time — the geometric series 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... sums to 1, not infinity

items.reveal_title: Zeno's paradoxes and the calculus that resolves them
items.reveal:
Zeno of Elea (c. 490-430 BC) offered several paradoxes about motion:
- Dichotomy: to walk across a room, you must first walk half-way, then half of what remains, etc. Infinite steps.
- Achilles and the tortoise: as above.
- Arrow: at each instant, an arrow occupies a fixed position, so it isn't moving — yet motion sums to a journey.

Resolution requires the concept of convergent infinite series — formalised in the 17th and 19th centuries by Newton, Leibniz, Cauchy and Weierstrass. The sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... equals 2, not infinity. Infinitely many tasks can be completed in finite time, provided their durations form a convergent series.

The paradoxes pre-dated rigorous calculus by 2000 years. Zeno's challenge actually pushed mathematicians toward developing the tools needed to handle infinity and the continuum properly. Mathematicians sometimes joke that Zeno was the first calculus student to fail to grasp limits.
items.why: Common sense rules out infinite tasks in finite time. Mathematical analysis shows infinite tasks of decreasing size can totalise to finite quantities — and motion proceeds.

items.title: Knowing the equations exactly doesn't let you predict the weather
items.claim: The atmosphere obeys Newton's laws, well-known fluid dynamics, well-known thermodynamics. Knowing all the equations doesn't let us predict beyond about 10 to 14 days. The system is deterministic but unpredictable.
items.prompt: How can determinism coexist with unpredictability?

options.text: In chaotic systems, infinitesimally different initial conditions diverge exponentially over time; predicting day 20 requires knowing today's conditions to a precision beyond physical measurement

items.reveal:
Edward Lorenz, simulating weather on a vacuum-tube computer in 1961, restarted a calculation from intermediate data printed to 3 decimal places. The internal precision was 6 places. The truncated and full simulations diverged completely within a simulated month.

He published the result in 1963 with a simplified 3-equation model showing strange attractor dynamics. His 1972 talk title — 'Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?' — gave us the butterfly effect.

The key insight: any uncertainty in initial conditions doubles every few days in the atmosphere. After 10 doublings — about 2 to 3 weeks — uncertainty in tiny details has grown to dominate the whole forecast.

Ensemble weather forecasting (running many simulations from slightly perturbed starts) addresses this by giving a probability distribution rather than a single prediction.
items.why: Determinism is conflated with predictability. Lorenz showed they are different: the equations may be exact and the system may still be unpredictable in practice, because small errors grow exponentially.
